title: Flowers instead
hookLine: legend says Hindus and Muslims fought over Kabir's body and found only flowers
tomorrow: how did a weaver's songs end up in someone else's scripture?

cards: Theo and his dad fought last night, over whether Theo will read the Bible at Hannah's wedding. Kabir's followers fought too, over his body.

The legend says that when Kabir died at Maghar, his Hindu followers wanted to cremate him, as Hindus do, and his Muslim followers wanted to bury him, as Muslims do. Voices rose. Someone lifted the sheet.
There was no body underneath. Only flowers.

teach.b: So they split the flowers. The Hindus burned their half; the Muslims buried theirs. Tradition says a Hindu shrine and a Muslim tomb still stand side by side at Maghar.
Today's question: who does a holy person belong to? Kabir answered it while he was alive.

teach.h: RAM OR RAHIM: THEY FIGHT, NEITHER KNOWS.
teach.b: In a song from the Bijak, he sings: the Hindu says Ram is dear to him, the Turk says Rahim, and the two fight to the death, and neither knows the secret. That's his teaching: one God, beyond the names people fight over.
The flowers are how his followers told that teaching after he was gone. Now a neighbor. The Sikh Janamsakhis, the stories of Guru Nanak's life, tell nearly the same scene.
As Guru Nanak lay dying at Kartarpur, Hindus and Muslims argued over his body.
He told them to lay flowers on either side of him: whichever side's flowers stayed fresh overnight could have their way.
In the morning both sides' flowers were fresh, and the body was gone. What they share: a holy person who won't be owned by one camp, and a quarrel ended with something you can't keep.

And one honest difference. Kabir's followers each took half home. For Sikhs, Guru Nanak isn't split between two faiths at all: he's the first Guru of a path of its own, with a line of Gurus after him.

how: At Maghar, tradition says, a Hindu samadhi and a Muslim tomb for Kabir stand side by side; Sikhs tell the Janamsakhi story of Guru Nanak's flowers when they remember his passing at Kartarpur.

games.q: two cousins argue over whose custom grandma's memorial should follow. what does the flowers legend offer them?
o: let the cousin who visited her most decide
find something both sides can honor, not win
skip the memorial so nobody gets upset
games.why: in the legend nobody wins the body. both sides honor him their own way, with the same flowers.

practice: Bring to mind one quarrel that's still open: a family thread, a friend gone quiet. Version a short message that offers something instead of winning something: a memory, a thanks, a photo.
Send it now, or save it for later; either way, let the version be your flowers.

wordCard.voice: Flowers instead: the legend of Kabir's death, where a fight over his body ends with flowers to share.

orig.note: Hindi: Maghar, the town where, in the legend, Kabir died and his body became flowers.

carryVoice: Your line: only flowers. In the legend, no side gets to keep him. That's six with Kabir.
